display.whats: All Torah eating measures are olive-bulk, except impurity and Yom Kippur; Yom Kippur's exception is the date-bulk
display.hint: A baraita teaches that every Torah eating measure defaults to an olive-bulk - so why do the impurity and Yom Kippur cases both depart from that default, and what does each verse's changed wording teach?
display.title: Olive-Bulk: the Torah's Default Eating Measure

learning.ahaMoment: The olive-bulk isn't one measure among several - it is the Torah's default for every eating prohibition. Impurity and Yom Kippur are the two exceptions, each triggered by its own verse departing from the ordinary eating language.
learning.memoryAnchor: Olive-bulk is the default; Yom Kippur's date-bulk is the exception the verse's changed wording creates.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does a baraita say that every Torah eating measure is an olive-bulk except for impurity and Yom Kippur, and why is the Yom Kippur measure specifically a large date?
learning.coreTension: Between the Torah's single default measure (olive-bulk) for all eating prohibitions and two verses (impurity, Yom Kippur) whose altered wording signals a departure from that default.
learning.coreMove: A baraita teaches that every Torah eating measure is an olive-bulk, except where the verse changes its wording; the Yom Kippur verse's unusual language ('shall not be afflicted' rather than 'shall eat') is exactly this kind of departure, so its measure becomes a large date. The Gemara then explains why both the impurity case and the Yom Kippur case are needed together: the impurity case alone might be dismissed as ordinary stylistic variation, while the Yom Kippur case establishes that deviant wording generally signals a changed measure.

takeaway.text: The olive-bulk is the Torah's default measure for eating prohibitions; only where a verse's wording departs from the ordinary eating language - as with impurity and Yom Kippur - do the Sages read that departure as signaling a different measure, which for Yom Kippur is the large date.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume Yom Kippur's date-bulk measure is an unconnected special case; in fact it departs from the same olive-bulk default every other eating prohibition uses, triggered by the verse's own unusual wording.

argumentFlow.label: All eating measures are an olive-bulk, with exceptions
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A baraita teaches that all Torah measures for eating are an olive-bulk, except where the verse changes its wording, prompting the Sages to change the measure. Impurity of foods and Yom Kippur are the two cases: the verse 'shall not be afflicted' (rather than 'eat') is why the Yom Kippur measure is a large date, not an olive.

argumentFlow.label: Why both impurity and Yom Kippur are needed as proofs
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara asks why the impurity case alone does not suffice to show that altered wording alters the measure. It answers that from impurity alone one might say that is simply the verse's style; the Yom Kippur case teaches the general principle that deviant wording signals a changed halacha.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners assume every Torah eating-prohibition is measured by an olive-bulk without exception.
misconceptions.correction: The baraita itself marks exceptions tied to the verse's wording: impure foods and Yom Kippur carry larger measures precisely because their verses depart from the usual language, which the Sages read as deliberately signaling a different measure.

visualizableElements.item: Olive-bulk as the Torah's default eating measure, with impurity and Yom Kippur as verse-triggered exceptions

quizSeeds.question: Why is the Yom Kippur measure a large date rather than the standard olive-bulk?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the verse changes its language: it says 'any soul which shall not be afflicted' rather than 'shall eat.' The altered wording signals to the Sages that the measure differs from the usual olive-bulk, so it is set at the volume of a large date.

quizSeeds.question: Why does the baraita need both the impurity case and the Yom Kippur case to make its point?
quizSeeds.answer: From the impurity verse alone, one might dismiss the unusual wording as mere stylistic variation. The Yom Kippur case establishes the general rule that whenever a verse deviates from standard language, it implies a corresponding change in the halacha.

sugyot.finalRuling: The default Torah measure for eating prohibitions is an olive-bulk; the Yom Kippur measure is a large date because the verse's wording departs from the ordinary eating language, signaling the Sages to set a different standard.

display.whats: Egg-bulk measures a food's impurity, derived from what the throat holds at once
display.hint: How does the Gemara derive that the impurity of foods is measured by an egg's bulk, why must someone who unwittingly ate forbidden fat record the exact amount, and why does the Gemara conclude that these measures are a received tradition from Sinai rather than a later enactment?
display.title: Deriving the Egg-Bulk Measure for a Food's Impurity

learning.ahaMoment: The egg-bulk measure for a food's impurity is not the general Torah default (olive-bulk) but a targeted correction the Sages drew from a doubled biblical phrase; and once such measures are grounded in oral Sinaitic tradition rather than freely deducible from the verse, an individual's own exact record of what he ate becomes indispensable insurance against a future court raising the liability threshold.
learning.memoryAnchor: Egg-bulk for food-impurity: derived from the doubled root 'food which may be eaten, food that comes from food,' pinned down by what the throat holds at once. Measures like this trace to Sinai, later forgotten and restored, not invented - so a forgotten fat-amount matters.
learning.learnerQuestion: How does the Gemara derive the egg-bulk measure for a food's impurity, and why should someone who unwittingly ate forbidden fat record the exact amount?
learning.coreTension: Between wanting a single verse to settle an exact quantity and the Gemara's repeated need to narrow an open-ended derivation (kid vs. egg, giant egg vs. tiny egg) until only the throat's real capacity decides it.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara works through candidate readings of the doubled phrase 'food which may be eaten, food that comes from food' until only a chicken's egg survives as the measure for a food's impurity, then generalizes: since such measures are themselves an ancient Sinaitic tradition (later forgotten and restored by the prophets, not newly legislated), a person who unwittingly ate forbidden fat should record the exact amount, since a future court could still revise the operative threshold.

takeaway.text: Precise Torah measures like the egg-bulk for food-impurity are not simply read off a verse; they are narrowed through argument and ultimately traced to a Sinaitic tradition that can be forgotten and later restored, which is exactly why one who ate a borderline amount of something forbidden should record it precisely.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume the Gemara's back-and-forth over a kid, a ben pekua, and various eggs is just verse-parsing that ends in a clean textual proof; in fact the textual derivation runs out (a tiny bird's egg cannot be excluded from the verse alone), and the Gemara falls back on Rabbi Abbahu's independent physical criterion - what the throat holds at once - to actually settle the measure.

argumentFlow.label: Deriving the egg-bulk measure for impure food
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Elazar derives the egg-bulk from 'food which may be eaten,' the doubled root teaching food that comes from food, namely a chicken egg. Challenges from a kid or a ben pekua are rejected because each still requires cutting or is not yet edible, leaving the egg as the model.

argumentFlow.label: Which egg sets the measure?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara presses that the egg might be the giant bar yokhani's egg, and answers that in doubt one takes the smaller included measure, yielding the chicken egg. When it presses that it could be a tiny bird's egg, the verse alone cannot decide, so this derivation is left incomplete.

argumentFlow.label: Abbahu's own basis: what the throat holds at once
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Abbahu gives his own derivation from 'food which may be eaten,' meaning food eaten at one time. The Sages estimated the esophagus holds no more than a chicken's egg at once, so that volume becomes the measure for the impurity of foods.

argumentFlow.label: Recording the measure of forbidden fat one ate
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who unwittingly ate forbidden fat should write down the exact amount, in case a future court revises the measure, so his liability can be reassessed against the standard in force.

argumentFlow.label: Why a smaller future measure would not obligate him
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara asks what revision is feared. If a future court lowered the threshold to a small olive, he would still not owe an offering, because the baraita teaches that an offering is brought only by one who repents from awareness of sin, not one swept in by a changed measure.

argumentFlow.label: An offering follows awareness, not a measure change
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara elaborates: one who does not repent from awareness brings no offering. So if the measures shrank, a person whose original amount only later counts as an olive would not be obligated, since his liability would stem from the rule change, not from his own awareness of having sinned.

argumentFlow.label: The real concern: a future larger measure
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rather, the worry is that a future court might raise the threshold, requiring a large olive. One should record how much he ate, because a later court might rule that his amount falls short of the new olive measure, exempting him, so the record protects against over-obligation.

argumentFlow.label: Reconciling 'increase' with the initial reading
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Returning to the first suggestion, the Gemara asks why Rabbi Elazar said 'increase the measure' rather than 'decrease' if the fear was a smaller future olive. It answers that 'increase' may refer to an increase in the number of offerings brought once the liability-measure is smaller.

argumentFlow.label: Measures of punishment are from Sinai
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that measures and punishments are halacha from Sinai. The Gemara objects that punishments are written explicitly in the Torah, and restates: it is the measures that determine liability for punishment that are the Sinaitic transmission.

argumentFlow.label: Were the measures from Sinai or from the court of Jabez?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A baraita records that measures of punishment are from Sinai; others attribute them to the court of Jabez. Since a prophet may introduce nothing new, the Gemara reconciles: the measures were given at Sinai, later forgotten, and then reestablished by the prophets, not newly invented.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners think 'measures and punishments are from Sinai' means the punishments themselves were orally transmitted.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara corrects this: the punishments are written explicitly in the Torah. What is transmitted from Sinai are the measures that determine liability for those punishments, which were later forgotten and reestablished by the prophets.

visualizableElements.item: Chicken-egg measure for a food's impurity, derived from what the throat holds at once

quizSeeds.question: How does the Gemara arrive at a chicken egg as the measure for the impurity of foods?
quizSeeds.answer: Rabbi Abbahu's accepted basis is that 'food which may be eaten' means food eaten at one time, and the Sages estimated the esophagus holds no more than a chicken's egg at once. The earlier derivation from 'food that comes from food' was left open because it could not exclude a tiny or giant egg.

quizSeeds.question: Why should someone who unwittingly ate forbidden fat record exactly how much he ate?
quizSeeds.answer: In case a future court raises the liability-measure. If a later court requires a larger olive, his recorded amount might fall short of the new threshold, exempting him. He cannot be newly obligated by a smaller future measure, since offerings follow awareness of sin, not a rule change.

quizSeeds.question: How does the Gemara reconcile that the measures of punishment are both from Sinai and from the court of Jabez?
quizSeeds.answer: Because a prophet may introduce nothing new, the measures must have originated at Sinai. Over time they were forgotten, and the court of Jabez and the prophets reestablished them, so Jabez restored rather than invented the measures.

sugyot.finalRuling: The measure for a food's ritual impurity is a chicken's egg, based on what the throat can hold at one time. One who unwittingly ate forbidden fat should record the exact amount eaten, since these measures trace to a Sinaitic tradition that a future court could still revise upward.

display.whats: Drinking measure on YK: a cheekful (male'o lugmav); how it is derived
display.hint: The drinking measure for YK liability is a cheekful (male'o lugmav), not a standard liquid measure. The Gemara derives and explains this unusual measure.
display.title: The Cheekful: YK Drinking Measure

learning.ahaMoment: The cheekful is the Gemara's acknowledgment that thirst is personal: what relieves one person may not relieve another, so the measure must follow the body.
learning.memoryAnchor: Cheekful = body-relative measure: YK drinking liability follows the individual, not a fixed volume.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why is the Yom Kippur drinking measure a cheekful (male'o lugmav) rather than a standard volume?
learning.coreTension: Between standard liquid measures (revi'it, etc.) used in most halakhic contexts and the body-relative cheekful used specifically for YK drinking liability.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara derives that 'affliction' by thirst is subjective: the amount that relieves thirst varies by person. Therefore the measure is body-relative (a cheekful) rather than fixed volume, calibrating the prohibition to the actual experience of relief.

takeaway.text: The YK drinking measure is body-relative (a cheekful) because the prohibition targets the relief of thirst-affliction, which is subjective; a fixed volume cannot capture individual variation in what constitutes genuine relief.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may expect a fixed volume like other liquid measures; understanding that the cheekful is calibrated to subjective relief explains the departure from standard measures.

argumentFlow.label: A cheekful means one cheek's worth in appearance
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The mishna makes one who drinks a cheekful liable. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains this is not two literally full cheeks but the amount that, pushed to one side, makes a single cheek appear full. The mishna's plural 'cheeks' means it looks like two cheeks full when viewed from one side.

argumentFlow.label: A baraita seems to require an actual cheekful
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A baraita lists the drinking measure: Beit Shammai a quarter-log, Beit Hillel two cheeks full, Rabbi Yehuda in Rabbi Eliezer's name like two cheeks full in appearance, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira a single gulp. Beit Hillel's 'two cheeks full' seems to mean a literal full mouth, against Shmuel.

argumentFlow.label: Distinguishing Beit Hillel from Rabbi Eliezer
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara rereads Beit Hillel as also meaning the appearance of two cheeks full, but then it would equal Rabbi Eliezer's view. It distinguishes them by a 'paltry cheekful,' slightly less than full: Beit Hillel requires a full cheek, Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable even for the lesser mouthful.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Hoshaya: this would be a Beit Shammai leniency
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Hoshaya objects that if Beit Hillel's measure is a single cheekful, then Beit Shammai's quarter-log is the larger and stricter measure, an unusual case of Beit Shammai being stringent. He asks why such a case is not listed in Eduyyot, where Beit Shammai's leniencies are collected; the answer continues on the next page.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners take 'a cheekful' to mean two literally stuffed cheeks of liquid.
misconceptions.correction: Shmuel explains it as the volume that fills one cheek when the liquid is pushed to a side, which only appears like a full mouth. The measure is one cheek's worth in appearance, not two cheeks crammed full.

visualizableElements.item: Drinking measure on YK: a cheekful (male'o lugmav)

quizSeeds.question: According to Shmuel, what does the mishna's 'cheekful' actually require?
quizSeeds.answer: Not two literally full cheeks, but enough liquid that when pushed to one side of the mouth it makes a single cheek appear full. The plural language means it should look like two cheeks full when viewed from one side, even though it is one cheek's worth.

quizSeeds.question: How do the Sages distinguish Beit Hillel's measure from Rabbi Eliezer's once both are read as 'the appearance of a cheekful'?
quizSeeds.answer: By the case of a paltry cheekful, slightly less than a full cheek. Beit Hillel holds one liable only for a full cheekful, while Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable even for the lesser, paltry mouthful.

rashiTranslations.he: כזית בינוני אכלתי שמא יבא בית דין
rashiTranslations.en: 'I ate a medium olive's-bulk,' lest a court come

rashiTranslations.he: ויפטרנו מקרבן ונמצא מביא חולין
rashiTranslations.en: and exempt him from the sacrifice, and he would turn out to be bringing non-sacred food

rashiTranslations.he: לעזרה: ה"ג עונשין מיכתב כתיבי
rashiTranslations.en: into the Temple courtyard. This is the correct reading: 'punishments are explicitly written' -

rashiTranslations.he: אלא הכי קאמר שיעורין של עונשין וכו'. שיעורי עונשין שעל ידן הוא ענוש הלכה למשה מסיני באיזה שיעור הוא ענוש: יעבץ.
rashiTranslations.en: 'rather, this is what he means: the measures of the punishments, etc.' - the measures of punishments, by which one is punished, are a law given to Moshe at Sinai, at what measure is he punished. 'Yaavetz' -

rashiTranslations.he: הוא עתניאל בן קנז: כמה ישתה. מדבית הלל קפריך: הכי גרסינן איכא בינייהו כמלא לוגמיו דחוק. לבית הלל בעינן
rashiTranslations.en: he is Otniel ben Kenaz. 'how much shall he drink' - he raises the difficulty from Beit Hillel's view. This is the correct reading: 'the difference between them is a tight cheekful.' For Beit Hillel we require

rashiTranslations.he: כדי שיסלקנו לצד אחד ויראה כמלא לוגמיו בריוח ולרבי אליעזר כמלא לוגמיו דחוק: אם כן. דלבית הלל מיחייב בכדי
rashiTranslations.en: enough that he could push it to one side and it would appear like a cheekful comfortably, and for Rabbi Eliezer a tight cheekful suffices. 'if so' - that for Beit Hillel he is liable with enough

rashiTranslations.he: שיסלקנו וכו' הוה ליה בציר מרביעית והויא לה מקולי בית שמאי וליתנייה במסכת עדיות גבי קולי בית שמאי שכולן שנויות שם:
rashiTranslations.en: that he could push aside, etc., this would be less than a revi'it, and this would be among the leniencies of Beit Shammai, and it should have been taught in Tractate Eduyot regarding the leniencies of Beit Shammai, all of which are stated there:

rashiTranslations.he: כי
rashiTranslations.en: This ('ki') continues on 80b.
